title: Data Races, Mutexes and Locks
summary: When two threads access the same data, at least one writes, and nothing synchronizes them, you have a **data race**: undefined behaviour. A **mutex** admits one thread at a time to a **critical section**. Lock it with RAII: `std::lock_guard`, `std::scoped_lock`, `std::unique_lock`. Beware **deadlock**.
ideas:
1. Reproduce the lost update, then fix it with a mutex. Time both versions.
2. Create a deadlock with two accounts transferring in opposite directions, then fix it with `std::scoped_lock`.
3. Build `ThreadSafeQueue<T>` with `push` and a `tryPop` that returns `std::optional<T>`.

cards.a:
Unsynchronized access to one variable, with at least one write

Data races are undefined behaviour. Concurrent reads alone are fine; a write without synchronization is not.

cards.q: How does `std::scoped_lock` prevent deadlock with several mutexes?
cards.a:
It locks them all together with a deadlock-avoiding algorithm

Two threads listing the same mutexes in different orders cannot deadlock, because `std::scoped_lock` never holds one while waiting forever for another.

cards.q: Why is calling `lock()` and `unlock()` directly dangerous?
cards.a:
An exception or early return between them leaves the mutex locked permanently

RAII locks such as `std::lock_guard` and `std::scoped_lock` unlock in their destructor on every path.

cards.q: Why does making every member function thread-safe not make every use of the class safe?
cards.a:
Another thread can act between two separate calls

`if (!q.empty()) q.pop();` can fail if another thread pops in between. Offer a combined `tryPop()` instead.
